newsitem.title: THAILAND: Baht effect on Thai oil seen offset by crude price.
newsitem.headline: Baht effect on Thai oil seen offset by crude price.

text.p: A downtrend in world crude oil prices and strong competition in Thailand's retail market will help minimise the effect of a de facto baht devaluation on oil prices in the near-term, industry and government sources said on Thursday.
The baht's recent float will boost local retail prices of oil, they said.

But the impact and magnitude of the expected local price increase will be more pronounced later this year when world crude prices are likely to rise on high demand due to the northern winter, the sources told Reuters.
However, higher local retail prices will have little impact on inflation in the near term, they said.

Sompong Amornvivat, minister in the prime minister's office in charge of energy policy, told Reuters that even with an anticipated rise in the cost of oil products of 25-30 satangs (8-10 cents) per litre, retail oil prices will still be lower than earlier this year because of softer crude prices.

"The impact of oil prices on consumer prices should be limited. After all, domestic oil prices were higher earlier this year and yet the government managed to keep inflation under control," Sompong said.
High crude prices earlier this year boosted retail diesel prices to 9.45 baht and gasoline to 9.75 baht per litre in January against 8.30 baht and 9.51 baht respectively in June.

Global benchmark Brent crude oil prices on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) peaked at $25.06 per barrel on October 15. Prices have fallen this year to $17.32 on June 11, the lowest level since May 20, 1996 when prices were as low as $16.75.
Dubai oil, widely purchased by Thai refineries, hit a peak of $22.84 per barrel on January 9, 1997 -- the highest level since the Gulf War.
The price fell to $16.10 on April 8 and April 10, the lowest level since May 20, 1996 when prices were $15.95.
Thailand on July 2 abolished a 13-year baht peg to a trade-weighted basket of currencies and introduced a managed float of the baht.
The baht depreciated by 15-20 percent after the float and analysts said the devalued baht was likely to put pressure on consumer prices.

Oil industry sources estimated that if the baht hovered around a level of 28.00-29.00 baht per dollar, retail oil prices would rise 25-50 satangs. If the currency weakened to 30 baht a dollar, the cost would rise to around 60-70 satang per litre.

"But I don't expect the baht to fall to that level because this is a managed float system under which the authority will step in to intervene if it deviated from the appropriate level," said Prasert Bunsumpun, president of PTT Oil.
The baht was quoted at 29.01/29.06 to the dollar late in the onshore market. In the offshore market, the currency was traded at 28.90/29.10 to the dollar late.
Prasert told Reuters that tough competition in Thailand's retail oil business will help keep oil prices reasonable as it would be difficult to make profits.
"The pump prices will reflect the crude prices and the exchange rate," he said.

"You cannot just mark up the prices at will because you could loose your clients given the high competition in the market," Prasert said, referring to the 30 oil companies and thousands of retail stations nationwide.
Prasert hailed the government's policy not to resort to retail oil price controls to curb inflation after the baht float.
Thailand floated its oil prices in 1991.
"It is impossible to float the exchange rate and control oil prices. If government agencies do their job properly, the impact of the float on consumer prices can be minimised," he said.
The government said it will not intervene to control oil prices and minister Sompong denied reports that refineries had been asked to cut their profit margins to keep prices stable.

"It is impossible to make such request. The refinery margins were already very low. We did ask oil companies to cut marketing margins if they could. But if not, we are not going to force them," Sompong said.
The marketing margin is the initial profit to be shared by refineries and retail stations. Market margins are around 60-90 satang per litre.
